title: Controlled Ansible recovery

environment.host: WSL2 (Linux) on Windows 11 with Docker Desktop

summary.headline: Silent failure (HTTP 200, 6/6 wrong results) detected as a correctness incident; the playbook's dry run changed 0 things, the real run finished in 17.4 s with result SUCCESS with no moment without a Ready pod, and the next request was correct=True.

timeline.event: scenario E started: baseline, 1 pod Ready
injected a silent failure: POST /simulate-failure {scenario: wrong_result}
6 requests all returned HTTP 200 but 6/6 results were wrong; /health says 'ok' and /ready says 'ready'; open incidents: correctness
dry run finished: DRY RUN (no changes made) (changes made: 0)
pod traceguard-6f8d5987fd-9crzg is no longer Ready
playbook finished: SUCCESS; post-recovery probe {'ready': 'ready', 'http_status': 200, 'correct': True, 'sku': 'E-100'}
after recovery: next request correct=True, injected fault state = none (reset with the process)

measurements.name: Dry run (--check): changes made
measurements.note: read-only checks only; the restart is reported as 'would run'

measurements.name: Real run: tasks ok / changed / failed
Real run: playbook wall time
measurements.note: includes waiting for the rolling update and the verification probe

measurements.name: Time with no Ready pod (observer, about 1 s resolution)
measurements.note: rolling update with maxUnavailable: 0 keeps the old pod Ready until the new one is

notes: One run on one laptop. The playbook is restricted to deployment traceguard in namespace traceguard of the kind-traceguard context; extra-vars cannot widen that (tested).
Rollback (recovery_action=rollback) exists and was verified locally; it is not part of this recording.
The injected fault lives in process memory, so any restart clears it. A restart does not fix a real bad release: that is what rollback is for.
